capabilities.target: Chat reply to the authenticated requester
Public web pages for reference links

inputs.source: Employee question via SSO-authenticated chat client
Engineering design docs returned by docs.search
Customer-filed Jira tickets, ingested via a planned Jira MCP server

elements.name: Design doc content entering the agent's context
Chat reply leaving the agent to the requester
Jira ticket content entering the agent's context
Outbound web fetch leaving the agent

controls.name: SSO authentication for the employee chat channel
Reply delivery bound to the authenticated requester
controls.decay_rationale: The reply destination is fixed by the chat platform to the authenticated requester of record, not chosen by the model, so it does not decay with model capability and cannot be redirected to an attacker-controlled recipient.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
No network egress capability in the current deployment
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the absence of any egress-capable tool today; this is exactly the control the planned web.fetch tool removes (new_tool trigger), independent of model capability.

controls.name: Write access to design docs restricted to engineers
System prompt instruction against pasting secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model's own judgment about what counts as a secret or credential; a more capable or injected model may rationalize an exception or be instructed to disregard the rule.

controls.name: Domain allowlist and query-parameter stripping on web.fetch
Untrusted-content handling for Jira MCP ticket input
Tamper-evident audit log of searches and replies

findings.title: Confidential design doc content reaching the chat reply is severed from exfiltration by recipient binding

attack_path.note: Confidential design doc content enters context via docs.search.
Read of confidential engineering design docs.
Content is included in a reply; is_egress and confidential sensitivity make this an S3 sink before controls.

forecast.watch_signal: Chat client configuration change that removes recipient binding, or reply routing logic modified to allow a configurable destination.

evidence.observation: Replies go only to the authenticated requester and the chat client does not render images or fetch links, binding the reply destination to the record and closing the rendered-link exfiltration channel.
Design docs are marked confidential, so content read via docs.search and included in a reply carries confidential sensitivity.

findings.title: No attributable record of which confidential document was disclosed to whom

forecast.watch_signal: New input sources (web.fetch, Jira MCP) go live without a corresponding audit-logging implementation.

evidence.observation: No artifact describes logging of docs.search queries, which document was returned, or which employee received which reply, so actions cannot be attributed after the fact.
The prompt instructs the agent to answer using docs.search and cite the document, but nothing requires that query and citation to be recorded outside the live chat reply.

recommendations.action: Add tamper-evident logging that records each docs.search query, the document retrieved, and the reply recipient, tied to the employee's SSO identity.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): planned web.fetch and Jira MCP server would let a customer-authored ticket exfiltrate confidential design docs

attack_path.note: Customer-authored Jira ticket content (untrusted) enters the agent's context once the Jira MCP server is connected; it can carry hidden instructions.
Injected instructions direct the agent to search confidential engineering design docs.
Confidential design doc content becomes part of the agent's working context.
Injected instructions direct the agent to fetch an attacker-controlled URL with the confidential content encoded in the query string, completing exfiltration.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: The read-only, least-privilege credential on docs.search (c.readonly_credential_docs_search) constrains the sink enough to earn one step of narrowing credit even though it does not cover the egress capability itself; no other declared control reaches cap.web_fetch or in.jira_tickets once the roadmap items exist.

forecast.watch_signal: docs.search credential scope widened beyond read-only, or the scoping control disabled without review.

evidence.observation: The roadmap adds a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server ingesting tickets filed by customers (untrusted), with no stated authentication, content handling, or egress restriction for either addition.
The only control currently blocking exfiltration is the absence of a network egress capability; the roadmap's web.fetch tool removes exactly that control.

recommendations.action: Before connecting the Jira MCP server, restrict web.fetch to a vetted domain allowlist and strip or reject model-constructed query parameters so confidential content cannot be smuggled out via the URL.

Treat all content from the Jira MCP server as untrusted: spotlight/delimit it, run it through an input injection classifier, and prevent it from triggering docs.search or web.fetch calls without the asking employee's explicit, separate request.
Pin and verify the Jira MCP server's identity and tool definitions before granting it access, consistent with the existing SSO-based trust model for employee input.

stride_coverage.rationale: Single internal agent process with no peer agents in this design; no artifact describes a mechanism by which another entity could impersonate docs-qa to employees or systems.
Artifacts do not describe how the deployed system prompt or configuration for docs-qa is protected against unauthorized modification outside deployment processes.
No rate limit, quota, or concurrency control for docs.search invocations is described, so resilience to a flood of questions cannot be assessed.

Artifacts state design docs are confidential and write-restricted to engineers, but do not state whether docs.search enforces per-employee read permissions or returns results to any authenticated employee regardless of role.
No rate limit or query quota on docs.search is described, so bulk scraping resilience cannot be assessed.
Transport integrity protections for chat replies between the agent and the chat platform are not described in the artifacts.
No rate limit on the number of replies sent per employee or per session is described in the artifacts.
No authentication, identity verification, or definition pinning is described for the planned Jira MCP server.
No logging design has been specified for the planned Jira integration in the roadmap note.
Ticket volume and its effect on agent resource usage are not described in the roadmap note.
Credential scope for the planned Jira MCP server connection is not described in the roadmap note.
Customer identity verification within the Jira ticketing system is outside the scope of the artifacts provided.
No mechanism is described for attributing which customer or ticket introduced content that reaches the agent.
No volume limit on ingested ticket content is described in the roadmap note.
No rate limit on outbound web fetches is described in the roadmap note.

rating.rationale: Present-day findings top out at high: the only sensitive present-day path (confidential design docs reaching the chat reply) is driven to low by recipient-bound reply delivery and a chat client that does not render links or images, but the agent has no attributable record of which document was disclosed to whom, which keeps residual at high on its own. The forecast reaches critical because the roadmap's two planned additions, a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server that ingests customer-filed tickets, would together open a lethal trifecta: untrusted ticket content could direct the agent to read confidential design docs and exfiltrate them via an attacker-controlled URL, and the only control that currently blocks this (no egress capability at all) is exactly what the new_tool trigger removes. No stated control would cover web.fetch or the Jira input once built.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no tool manifest, MCP config, or logs were available to verify the implementation.

No artifact describes whether docs.search enforces per-employee read permissions on confidential design docs beyond the stated write restriction to engineers; this is noted as a STRIDE gap rather than assumed safe.

The planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are described only in a one-line roadmap note; their capability scope, credential handling, and any planned controls are inferred and carry medium confidence.
